questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 28-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a motorcycle accident. Examination reveals that his right arm is held in adduction and internal rotation with the elbow extended. He is unable to abduct or externally rotate the shoulder. Sensation is lost over the lateral aspect of the shoulder. Which nerve is most likely injured?

options.B: Axillary nerve
options.D: Long thoracic nerve

questions.explanation: Correct (B – Axillary nerve): The axillary nerve (C5, C6) wraps around the surgical neck of the humerus and is the most commonly injured nerve in anterior shoulder dislocation. It supplies the deltoid (shoulder abduction) and teres minor (external rotation), and provides cutaneous supply to the 'regimental badge area' over the lateral shoulder. The posture described — adduction + internal rotation + elbow extension — is the 'policeman's tip' but is milder here, affecting only the axillary territory. Incorrect options: (A) Radial nerve injury causes wrist drop; it is injured in mid-shaft humeral fractures, not shoulder dislocation. (C) Musculocutaneous nerve injury causes weakness of elbow flexion and loss of sensation over the lateral forearm. (D) Long thoracic nerve injury causes winging of the scapula. Exam pearl: Always test deltoid power and regimental badge area sensation after any shoulder dislocation.

questions.image_title: MRI of the knee joint showing structure passing through intercondylar notch
questions.question_text: A 25-year-old football player presents with acute knee pain after a tackle. Examination shows a positive anterior drawer test and a positive Lachman test. MRI of the knee is shown. Which of the following statements about the structure most likely injured is CORRECT?

options.A: It attaches from the posterior intercondylar area of the tibia to the medial surface of the lateral femoral condyle
options.B: It attaches from the anterior intercondylar area of the tibia to the lateral surface of the medial femoral condyle
options.C: It prevents posterior displacement of the femur on the tibia
options.D: It is supplied primarily by the lateral genicular artery

questions.explanation: Correct (B – ACL attachment): Positive anterior drawer and Lachman tests indicate ACL rupture. The ACL runs from the anterior intercondylar area of the tibia (in front of the tibial spine) upward, backward, and laterally to attach to the posterior part of the medial surface of the lateral femoral condyle. Incorrect options: (A) Describes the PCL — it attaches posteriorly on the tibia and to the medial femoral condyle's lateral surface. (C) The ACL prevents anterior tibial displacement (not posterior femoral displacement). The PCL prevents posterior tibial displacement. (D) The ACL is supplied by the middle genicular artery (also called the middle geniculate), not lateral genicular. Exam pearl: ACL – Anterior, tibial attachment is Anterior, goes to Lateral condyle. PCL is the reverse. Most common sports injury in young adults.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 55-year-old woman presents with inability to close her right eye, deviation of the angle of mouth to the left, and loss of taste over the anterior two-thirds of the right tongue. She also reports hyperacusis on the right side. Where is the MOST LIKELY site of the lesion?

options.A: Internal acoustic meatus (proximal to geniculate ganglion)
options.B: Between geniculate ganglion and origin of chorda tympani
options.D: Parotid gland region

questions.explanation: Correct (A): The lesion must be proximal to ALL branches of the facial nerve. The patient has: (1) LMN facial palsy (CN VII motor), (2) loss of taste on anterior 2/3 tongue (chorda tympani branch), (3) hyperacusis (nerve to stapedius). The nerve to stapedius branches off between the geniculate ganglion and the origin of chorda tympani. Since hyperacusis is present, the lesion must be at or proximal to the nerve to stapedius — placing it in the internal acoustic meatus (proximal to the geniculate ganglion) or at the geniculate ganglion itself. Incorrect options: (B) Lesion between geniculate ganglion and chorda tympani would spare the greater superficial petrosal nerve (no dry eye) but would cause hyperacusis + taste loss. However, since lacrimation was not mentioned, this could be a trap. The most proximal site that explains all findings including hyperacusis is the IAM. (C) Below stylomastoid foramen: only motor branches affected; taste and hyperacusis are spared. (D) Parotid lesion: only distal motor branches affected. Exam pearl: Map CN VII branches from proximal to distal — GGSMC: Greater petrosal nerve, Nerve to stapedius, Chorda tympani, Motor branches.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 45-year-old man undergoes a posterolateral thoracotomy. During surgery, the surgeon needs to avoid injury to the neurovascular bundle. In which part of the intercostal space does the main intercostal nerve and vessels run?

options.B: Lower border of each rib in the costal groove
options.D: Along the outer surface of the internal intercostal muscle

questions.explanation: Correct (B): The intercostal neurovascular bundle (vein, artery, nerve — VAN from above downward) runs in the costal groove on the inner surface of the upper rib at the lower border. This is why thoracocentesis and pleural aspiration needles are inserted just above the upper border of the lower rib of a given space to avoid these structures. Incorrect options: (A) Upper border: no neurovascular bundle here — used as the safe needle entry point in pleural aspiration. (C) Middle of the space: incorrect anatomical position. (D) The bundle runs deep to the innermost intercostal muscle, between it and the internal intercostal. Exam pearl: VAN mnemonic — Vein (most superior), Artery, Nerve (most inferior) in the costal groove.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: During an open appendectomy, the surgeon identifies the appendix by tracing the taenia coli of the cecum. A 30-year-old woman undergoing this procedure is found to have the appendix lying in a retrocecal position. Which of the following symptoms would this patient MOST LIKELY present with, explaining the unusual clinical picture?

options.A: Guarding in the right iliac fossa with positive Rovsing sign
options.B: Psoas sign positive with pain referred to right thigh/hip flexion
options.C: Obturator sign positive with suprapubic tenderness
options.D: Left iliac fossa pain due to referred mesenteric pain

questions.explanation: Correct (B): A retrocecal appendix lies posterior to the cecum and is in contact with the iliopsoas (psoas major) muscle. Inflammation irritates the psoas, leading to a positive psoas sign (pain on passive extension of the right hip with patient lying on left side). Pain may also be referred to the right thigh. Incorrect options: (A) Guarding in RIF and Rovsing sign are typical of the common iliac/pelvic position of the appendix. (C) Positive obturator sign (pain on internal rotation of the flexed right hip) is characteristic of a pelvic appendix irritating the obturator internus. (D) Appendicitis does not typically cause left-sided pain regardless of position. Exam pearl: Most common position of appendix = Retrocecal (65%). Clinical signs depend on position: Retrocecal → Psoas sign; Pelvic → Obturator sign; Promontoric → Rovsing sign positive.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 60-year-old man presents with progressive hoarseness of voice. On laryngoscopy, the left vocal cord is immobile in the paramedian position. CT chest reveals a large left hilar mass. Which anatomical course of the relevant nerve BEST explains this finding?

options.A: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the arch of aorta at the level of the ligamentum arteriosum
options.B: The right recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the arch of aorta
options.C: The left superior laryngeal nerve is compressed by the hilar mass
options.D: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops around the left common carotid artery

questions.explanation: Correct (A): The left recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) has a longer intrathoracic course than the right. It loops under the arch of the aorta at the level of the ligamentum arteriosum (just lateral to the aortic arch) before ascending in the tracheoesophageal groove to reach the larynx. A left hilar lung mass, lymph node enlargement (e.g., from lung cancer), or aortic aneurysm can compress it at this site, causing left vocal cord palsy (Ortner syndrome when due to cardiovascular causes). The vocal cord lies in a paramedian (cadaveric) position when the RLN is completely paralysed. Incorrect options: (B) The right RLN loops around the right subclavian artery in the neck/upper thorax — far from a left hilar mass. (C) The superior laryngeal nerve supplies the cricothyroid and sensation above the cords — its injury causes subtle voice fatigue, not complete cord palsy. (D) The RLN does not loop around the common carotid. Exam pearl: Left RLN injury → aortic arch pathology, left lung cancer, left hilar nodes. Right RLN injury → right subclavian/right apical pathology.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A neonate is diagnosed with persistent truncus arteriosus. The echocardiogram reveals a single arterial trunk arising from both ventricles with a large VSD. Which embryological structure has FAILED to develop normally?

options.B: Aorticopulmonary septum
options.D: Sinus venosus

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Truncus arteriosus normally divides into the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk through the formation of the aorticopulmonary septum (spiral septum). This septum grows in a spiral fashion within the truncus arteriosus. Failure of this septum to form results in persistent truncus arteriosus — a single arterial trunk receiving blood from both ventricles, associated with a VSD. Incorrect options: (A) Endocardial cushions contribute to the formation of the AV valves and the membranous part of the interventricular septum. Defects here cause AV canal defects and membranous VSDs. (C) The muscular part of the interventricular septum develops by upgrowth from the ventricular floor; its failure causes muscular VSD, not truncus arteriosus. (D) Sinus venosus abnormalities cause sinus venosus ASD and anomalous pulmonary venous drainage. Exam pearl: Aorticopulmonary septum spirals 180° — explains why aorta and pulmonary artery spiral around each other. DiGeorge syndrome (22q11 deletion) is associated with truncus arteriosus.

questions.image_title: Cross-section of spinal cord at thoracic level showing tract locations
key_findings: Dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus) in posterior funiculus
Lateral corticospinal tract in lateral funiculus
Anterior spinothalamic tract in anterior funiculus
Lateral spinothalamic tract in lateral funiculus
questions.question_text: A 35-year-old man presents with loss of pain and temperature sensation on the RIGHT side below the umbilicus, with loss of touch, vibration, and proprioception on the LEFT side below the umbilicus. The LEFT leg also shows upper motor neuron signs. The RIGHT leg is normal neurologically. At which spinal cord level and what type of lesion is MOST consistent with these findings?

options.A: Left half of spinal cord transected at T10 (Brown-Séquard syndrome)
options.B: Right half of spinal cord transected at T10 (Brown-Séquard syndrome)
options.C: Complete transection of spinal cord at T10
options.D: Central cord syndrome at T10

questions.explanation: Correct (A): This is a classic Brown-Séquard syndrome presentation. Left-sided hemisection at T10 causes: (1) Ipsilateral (left) loss of dorsal column functions (touch, vibration, proprioception) — these fibres ascend ipsilaterally before crossing in the medulla. (2) Ipsilateral (left) UMN signs — corticospinal fibres have already crossed in the medulla. (3) Contralateral (right) loss of pain and temperature — lateral spinothalamic tract fibres cross within 1–2 segments of entry. Incorrect options: (B) Right half hemisection would give right-sided dorsal column loss and left-sided spinothalamic loss — the reverse of what is described. (C) Complete transection causes bilateral loss of all modalities below the level. (D) Central cord syndrome affects upper limbs more than lower limbs (cape-like distribution); UMN signs are bilateral. Exam pearl: Brown-Séquard = ipsilateral UMN + dorsal column loss + contralateral spinothalamic loss. Most common cause: penetrating trauma or MS plaque.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A carpenter presents with inability to flex the distal interphalangeal joints of the index and middle fingers. He can flex the proximal interphalangeal joints normally. He also has weakness of pronation of the forearm. Which nerve is most likely injured and where?

options.B: Median nerve at the wrist (carpal tunnel)
options.D: Radial nerve at the lateral epicondyle

questions.explanation: Correct (C): The anterior interosseous nerve (AIN) is a pure motor branch of the median nerve arising below the elbow. It supplies: FDP to index and middle fingers, FPL, and pronator quadratus. AIN syndrome causes: (1) Inability to flex distal phalanx of index/middle (FDP), (2) Inability to flex distal phalanx of thumb (FPL), (3) Weakness of forearm pronation (pronator quadratus) — classic sign is inability to make 'OK' sign. Incorrect options: (A) Ulnar nerve at wrist: causes loss of intrinsic hand muscles (interossei, hypothenar) and sensory loss on ulnar 1.5 fingers — not FDP weakness. (B) Median nerve at carpal tunnel: affects thenar muscles and sensation in lateral 3.5 fingers; FDP and pronation are proximal to this level. (D) Radial nerve at lateral epicondyle: causes posterior interosseous nerve issues — wrist/finger extension weakness. Exam pearl: AIN syndrome = no sensory loss (pure motor). Test: 'pinch' mechanism — patient makes a circle with thumb and index; in AIN palsy, both hyperextend at IP joints.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 62-year-old woman undergoes a total hip replacement. Postoperatively, she develops foot drop and loss of sensation over the dorsum of the foot and lateral leg. Which nerve was most likely injured during surgery?

options.B: Obturator nerve
options.D: Tibial nerve

questions.explanation: Correct (C): The common peroneal nerve is the most commonly injured nerve during hip replacement surgery. It winds around the neck of the fibula where it is superficial and vulnerable. Its injury causes: foot drop (weakness of dorsiflexion and eversion — deep and superficial peroneal branches), and sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot and anterolateral leg. Incorrect options: (A) Femoral nerve injury causes quadriceps weakness (inability to extend knee) and loss of sensation over anteromedial thigh/knee — not foot drop. (B) Obturator nerve injury causes weakness of hip adduction and medial thigh sensory loss. (D) Tibial nerve injury causes plantar flexion and inversion weakness; sensory loss over the sole of the foot — not foot drop. Exam pearl: Common peroneal nerve is the most commonly injured nerve in the lower limb overall. It wraps around the fibular neck — a surgical danger zone in posterior hip and knee approaches.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A neonate presents with bilious vomiting on day 2 of life. X-ray abdomen shows the 'double bubble' sign with no gas in the rest of the abdomen. At which embryological stage and due to failure of which process does this condition arise?

options.A: Failure of recanalization of the duodenum at 8–10 weeks
options.B: Failure of recanalization of the jejunum at 6–8 weeks
options.C: Failure of rotation of the midgut loop at 10 weeks
options.D: Failure of descent of the stomach at 6 weeks

questions.explanation: Correct (A): The 'double bubble' sign (two air-filled pouches — stomach and proximal duodenum) with no distal gas is pathognomonic of duodenal atresia. The duodenum undergoes a solid phase (epithelial proliferation obliterates the lumen) at 5–6 weeks, followed by recanalization at 8–10 weeks. Failure of recanalization leads to complete duodenal obstruction. Associated with Down syndrome (trisomy 21) in ~30% of cases. Incorrect options: (B) Jejunal atresia is due to intrauterine vascular accidents (not a recanalization failure) and shows multiple air-fluid levels with 'triple bubble' or 'soap bubble' pattern. (C) Midgut malrotation causes volvulus and intermittent bilious vomiting; the X-ray shows abnormal small bowel position. (D) The stomach does not have a solid phase — its obstruction (pyloric stenosis) is muscular hypertrophy, not atresia, and presents at 3–6 weeks of age with non-bilious vomiting. Exam pearl: Duodenal atresia = Double bubble + Down syndrome + bilious vomiting after first feed.

key_findings: Cilia present at the apical surface
Goblet cells interspersed among columnar cells
All cells reach the basement membrane
Nuclei at different levels giving pseudostratified appearance
questions.question_text: A biopsy specimen from the trachea of a patient with chronic cough is shown above. Which of the following statements about this epithelial type is CORRECT?

options.A: All cells reach the luminal surface and the basement membrane
options.B: All cells reach the basement membrane but not all reach the luminal surface
options.C: Cells are arranged in two distinct layers with a shared basement membrane
options.D: It is the same epithelium lining the ureters and urinary bladder

questions.explanation: Correct (B): The image shows pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium (respiratory epithelium). The key defining feature is that ALL cells touch the basement membrane, but only TALL cells reach the luminal surface. Short basal cells do not reach the surface. This creates the false appearance of stratification (hence 'pseudo-stratified'). Nuclei appear at different heights giving the stratified look. Incorrect options: (A) In simple epithelium, every cell touches both surfaces — not pseudostratified. (C) True stratified epithelium has multiple layers; only the basal layer contacts the basement membrane. (D) The urinary bladder and ureter are lined by transitional epithelium (urothelium), which can stretch and has dome-shaped surface cells. Exam pearl: Respiratory epithelium locations — trachea, bronchi, most of the nasal cavity. It transitions to simple cuboidal in bronchioles. Kartagener syndrome causes ciliary dysfunction affecting this epithelium.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 42-year-old woman undergoes a radical hysterectomy for cervical carcinoma. Postoperatively, she develops urinary incontinence and is unable to feel bladder fullness. CT imaging shows the ureter has been transected 1 cm lateral to the cervix. Which anatomical relationship explains why the ureter was injured at this site?

options.A: The ureter passes above the uterine artery at the level of the cervix
options.B: The uterine artery crosses above the ureter at the level of the cervix (ureter is water under the bridge)
options.C: The ureter passes through the broad ligament lateral to the cervix at all levels
options.D: The ureter passes posterior to the ovarian artery near the cervix

questions.explanation: Correct (B): The most clinically critical anatomical relationship in the female pelvis is that the uterine artery crosses ABOVE the ureter at the level of the cervix (approximately 2 cm lateral to the cervix at the level of the internal os). This is described as 'water (ureter) under the bridge (uterine artery).' During hysterectomy, when the surgeon ligates the uterine artery, the ureter is at risk of being cut, kinked, or ligated. This is the most common site of iatrogenic ureteric injury in gynecological surgery. Incorrect options: (A) The reverse is true — the uterine artery is ABOVE (crosses over) the ureter. (C) The ureter runs in the base of the broad ligament medially, not throughout its lateral extent. (D) The ovarian artery/vein run in the suspensory ligament of the ovary (infundibulopelvic ligament) in the upper pelvis — not near the cervix. Exam pearl: 'Water under the bridge' is a mandatory exam fact. Ureteric injury most common at: (1) where it crosses over the pelvic brim, (2) near the uterine artery, (3) near the vaginal vault.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 70-year-old man presents with involuntary, large-amplitude, flinging movements of his right arm and leg. MRI brain shows a small hemorrhagic lesion on the LEFT side. Which structure is most likely damaged?

options.B: Left globus pallidus interna
options.D: Left putamen

questions.explanation: Correct (C): The clinical picture describes hemiballismus — large amplitude, proximal, flinging (ballistic) movements affecting the contralateral limbs. The subthalamic nucleus (STN) of Luys is the classic lesion site for hemiballismus. The STN normally has an excitatory (glutamatergic) effect on the globus pallidus interna (GPi). When the STN is damaged, GPi loses its drive, thalamic activity is disinhibited, and excessive/uncontrolled movements result. The lesion is contralateral because the motor pathways decussate. Incorrect options: (A) Caudate nucleus lesions are associated with Huntington's disease (choreiform movements) — but Huntington's is bilateral and genetic. (B) GPi lesions would actually REDUCE movements (since GPi inhibits thalamus) — causing parkinsonism. (D) Putamen lesions cause contralateral hemiparesis or are associated with Parkinson's disease pathology. Exam pearl: Hemiballismus = STN lesion (contralateral). Most common cause: small vessel disease (lacunar infarct) in elderly hypertensives. STN is also a target in deep brain stimulation for Parkinson's disease.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 25-year-old man sustains a stab wound to the posterior triangle of the neck. Examination reveals a winged scapula. Which nerve is most likely injured?

options.B: Long thoracic nerve
options.D: Suprascapular nerve

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Winged scapula is caused by weakness of serratus anterior, which is supplied by the long thoracic nerve (C5, C6, C7 — 'C5, 6, 7 — bells of heaven'). The long thoracic nerve runs superficially along the lateral thoracic wall and is vulnerable to injury in the posterior triangle of the neck and during axillary dissection. Serratus anterior holds the scapula against the thoracic wall; its weakness allows the medial border to wing outward. Incorrect options: (A) Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) injury causes weakness of trapezius and SCM, presenting with drooping shoulder, inability to shrug, and difficulty turning head — NOT winged scapula primarily. It also runs in the posterior triangle but causes a different deficit. (C) Dorsal scapular nerve supplies rhomboids; its injury causes winging that is worse during retraction, not the classic presentation. (D) Suprascapular nerve supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus; its injury causes weakness of shoulder abduction and external rotation — not winging. Exam pearl: Long thoracic nerve injury → winging of scapula (medial border protrudes). Classic causes: radical mastectomy, posterior triangle injury, carrying heavy loads on shoulder.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 50-year-old man with a mid-shaft fracture of the humerus develops wrist drop. He also has sensory loss over the dorsum of the hand and the lateral 3.5 fingers. Which of the following muscles would be SPARED in this injury?

options.B: Brachioradialis
options.D: Triceps brachii

questions.explanation: Correct (D): A mid-shaft (spiral groove) radial nerve injury occurs BELOW the branches to the triceps. The triceps brachii is supplied by branches of the radial nerve that arise in the axilla (above the spiral groove), so it is SPARED in mid-shaft fractures. The patient can still extend the elbow. Muscles affected: brachioradialis, extensor carpi radialis longus/brevis, extensor digitorum, and all posterior interosseous nerve territories. Incorrect options: (A) ECRL is innervated by the radial nerve just below the elbow; it may be partially affected depending on fracture level. At mid-shaft level, it is usually affected. (B) Brachioradialis is the first muscle innervated in the forearm by the radial nerve — affected. (C) Extensor digitorum is innervated by the posterior interosseous nerve (deep branch of radial nerve) — affected. Exam pearl: Key rule for radial nerve: Axilla lesion = all muscles affected including triceps; Spiral groove = triceps SPARED; Lateral epicondyle = wrist extensors spared, only posterior interosseous territory affected.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A male infant is born with bilateral undescended testes (cryptorchidism). The testes are palpable in the inguinal canal. Which hormone produced by the fetal testes is primarily responsible for the initial phase of testicular descent into the inguinal canal?

options.B: Dihydrotestosterone (DHT)
options.D: Anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH)

questions.explanation: Correct (C): Testicular descent occurs in two phases. Phase 1 (transabdominal, 8–15 weeks): INSL3 (Insulin-like factor 3, also called relaxin-like factor) produced by Leydig cells acts on the gubernaculum, causing it to differentiate and shorten/thicken, anchoring the testis and pulling it toward the inguinal canal. Phase 2 (inguinoscrotal, 25–35 weeks): Testosterone (converted to DHT) drives the inguinoscrotal descent through the inguinal canal into the scrotum. Incorrect options: (A) Testosterone drives Phase 2 (inguinoscrotal descent), not Phase 1. (B) DHT (via 5-alpha reductase) drives Phase 2 and external genitalia virilization; NOT Phase 1. (D) AMH (from Sertoli cells) causes regression of the Müllerian ducts — it is not involved in testicular descent. Exam pearl: Bilateral cryptorchidism increases risk of testicular cancer and infertility. Orchidopexy recommended before age 2 years. AMH = Müllerian inhibiting substance (MIS).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 55-year-old man undergoes a coronary angiography. The right coronary artery is found to be dominant. Which of the following structures is MOST LIKELY supplied by the posterior descending artery (PDA) arising from the RCA in this patient?

options.B: AV node and posterior one-third of interventricular septum
options.C: Anterior two-thirds of interventricular septum and anterior papillary muscle
options.D: Left ventricular apex and lateral wall

questions.explanation: Correct (B): In a right-dominant circulation (present in ~70% of people), the RCA gives off the posterior descending artery (PDA), which supplies the AV node and the posterior one-third of the interventricular septum, as well as the posterior papillary muscle. AV node is supplied by the RCA in 90% of people (via the AV nodal artery). This explains why inferior MI (RCA territory) can cause AV conduction blocks. Incorrect options: (A) SA node is supplied by the RCA in 60% and LCA in 40%, but this is not the primary PDA territory. (C) The anterior 2/3 of the interventricular septum and anterior papillary muscle are supplied by the LAD (left anterior descending from LCA). (D) The left ventricular lateral wall is supplied by the obtuse marginal branches of the LCx (left circumflex). Exam pearl: PDA supplies the AV node and posterior septum regardless of dominance. Right dominance: PDA from RCA (~70%). Left dominance: PDA from LCx (~15%). Co-dominance (~15%).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 22-year-old woman is diagnosed with Marfan syndrome. The mutation affects fibrillin-1, which is an important component of which connective tissue structure?

options.B: Elastic fibers (microfibrils)
options.D: Ground substance proteoglycans

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Fibrillin-1 is a glycoprotein that forms the microfibrillar scaffold (sheath) of elastic fibers. In Marfan syndrome (autosomal dominant mutation in FBN1 gene on chromosome 15), abnormal fibrillin-1 leads to defective elastic fibers, causing the characteristic features: arachnodactyly, tall stature, lens subluxation (ectopia lentis), and most dangerously, aortic root dilation with risk of dissection. Incorrect options: (A) Type I collagen mutations cause osteogenesis imperfecta (brittle bone disease). (C) Type III collagen mutations cause Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (vascular type). (D) Ground substance proteoglycan abnormalities are seen in mucopolysaccharidoses (e.g., Hurler syndrome). Exam pearl: Marfan = fibrillin-1 (FBN1 gene, chr 15). Ehlers-Danlos = collagen synthesis/processing defects. Osteogenesis imperfecta = type I collagen defects.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 45-year-old man undergoes thyroid surgery. Postoperatively, he develops stridor and respiratory distress. On examination, bilateral loss of voice with high-pitched inspiratory stridor is noted. Which structure was most likely bilaterally injured?

options.A: External branch of superior laryngeal nerve
options.B: Internal branch of superior laryngeal nerve
options.D: Hypoglossal nerve

questions.explanation: Correct (C): Bilateral RLN injury causes bilateral vocal cord palsy. Each cord adopts the paramedian position (partially adducted), causing airway obstruction (stridor, respiratory distress) because the glottis cannot open adequately for inspiration. Voice is present but altered (bilateral cord involvement = bilateral adductor and abductor paralysis). Unilateral RLN injury: hoarseness only. Bilateral injury: life-threatening airway compromise requiring emergency tracheostomy. Incorrect options: (A) External branch of SLN supplies cricothyroid only (tensor of vocal cords). Bilateral injury causes loss of high-pitched phonation and voice fatigue — no stridor. (B) Internal branch of SLN is purely sensory for the larynx above the cords — bilateral injury causes aspiration, not stridor. (D) Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) supplies tongue muscles — bilateral injury causes dysarthria and dysphagia, not stridor. Exam pearl: Bilateral RLN palsy = emergency. Cord in paramedian position = complete RLN palsy. Cord in lateral position (cadaveric) = combined RLN + SLN palsy.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 60-year-old man with prostate cancer develops bone metastases. A bone biopsy shows increased osteoblastic activity with new bone formation. Which cell type is primarily responsible for bone RESORPTION in a normal bone remodeling cycle?

options.B: Osteocytes
options.D: Chondroblasts

questions.explanation: Correct (C): Osteoclasts are large, multinucleated cells (derived from monocyte/macrophage lineage) responsible for bone resorption. They create a sealing zone (clear zone) and a ruffled border where they secrete H+ ions (via carbonic anhydrase II) and lysosomal enzymes (cathepsin K) to dissolve mineral and digest organic matrix. They create Howship's lacunae on bone surfaces. Incorrect options: (A) Osteoblasts synthesize osteoid (Type I collagen) and are responsible for bone FORMATION, not resorption. In prostate cancer metastases, osteoblastic (sclerotic) lesions predominate — these show increased osteoblast activity. (B) Osteocytes are mature osteoblasts embedded in lacunae; they maintain matrix, detect mechanical stress, and regulate calcium homeostasis through sclerostin — they do not primarily resorb bone. (D) Chondroblasts form cartilage, not bone. Exam pearl: Bone remodeling sequence: Osteoclasts resorb → Osteoblasts fill in. Bisphosphonates inhibit osteoclasts. RANK-L/OPG pathway controls osteoclast activity.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A surgeon performing a Whipple's procedure (pancreaticoduodenectomy) needs to divide the gastroduodenal artery. From which artery does the gastroduodenal artery most commonly arise?

options.B: Splenic artery
options.D: Left gastric artery

questions.explanation: Correct (C): The gastroduodenal artery (GDA) arises from the common hepatic artery (a branch of the celiac trunk) before the common hepatic divides into the proper hepatic and right gastric arteries. The GDA then gives off the superior pancreaticoduodenal artery (supplies the head of pancreas and duodenum) and the right gastroepiploic artery. During Whipple's procedure, the GDA is a key surgical landmark. Incorrect options: (A) The SMA gives off the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery — not the GDA. The head of pancreas has dual blood supply from both superior (GDA via celiac) and inferior (SMA) pancreaticoduodenal arteries. (B) The splenic artery runs along the upper border of the pancreas and supplies the body and tail. It gives off the short gastric arteries and terminates in the spleen. (D) The left gastric artery (from celiac trunk) supplies the lesser curvature of the stomach — not the GDA. Exam pearl: Celiac trunk branches = Left gastric + Splenic + Common hepatic. Common hepatic → Proper hepatic + GDA. GDA → Superior pancreaticoduodenal + Right gastroepiploic.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 65-year-old woman presents with sudden onset of ipsilateral limb ataxia, ipsilateral Horner's syndrome, dysphagia, hoarseness, and loss of pain and temperature on the contralateral body and ipsilateral face. MRI reveals an infarct in the lateral medulla. Which artery is most likely occluded?

options.B: Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA)
options.D: Vertebral artery at its origin

questions.explanation: Correct (B): This is a classic Wallenberg syndrome (lateral medullary syndrome) caused by PICA occlusion (or vertebral artery occlusion, which is actually more common). PICA supplies the lateral medulla. Deficits: (1) Ipsilateral: Horner's syndrome (sympathetic pathway), cerebellar signs (inferior cerebellar peduncle), loss of pain/temperature on FACE (CN V nucleus), dysphagia/hoarseness (CN IX, X nuclei); (2) Contralateral: loss of pain/temperature on body (spinothalamic tract). Note: 'alternating hemianesthesia' = ipsilateral face + contralateral body pain/temperature loss. Incorrect options: (A) AICA syndrome affects the pons (lower), causing ipsilateral facial palsy (CN VII), deafness (CN VIII), and cerebellar signs — differs from PICA syndrome. (C) Basilar artery occlusion causes 'locked-in syndrome' — bilateral motor paralysis with preserved consciousness and eye movements. (D) Vertebral artery occlusion at origin can cause Wallenberg syndrome too, but PICA is the classic teaching answer. Exam pearl: PICA = LATERAL medullary syndrome (Wallenberg). AICA = lateral PONTINE syndrome. Basilar = locked-in.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 30-year-old man presents with inability to extend the metacarpophalangeal joints of the fingers while the interphalangeal joints can be extended normally. He also has sensory loss over a small area of skin on the dorsum of the hand near the first web space. Where is the lesion most likely located?

options.B: Posterior interosseous nerve in the radial tunnel
options.C: Radial nerve at the spiral groove of the humerus
options.D: Superficial radial nerve at the wrist

questions.explanation: Correct (B): The posterior interosseous nerve (PIN) is the deep motor branch of the radial nerve arising in the radial tunnel (at the lateral elbow, passing through supinator). PIN supplies all finger and thumb extensors. Its injury causes: finger drop at MCP level (cannot extend MCPs). IP extension is preserved because lumbricals (median/ulnar) extend IPs via the extensor hood. Key point: wrist extension is PARTIALLY preserved (ECRL is spared as it is innervated proximal to PIN origin). Sensory loss in the first web space (posterior cutaneous territory of the radial nerve's superficial branch) suggests a slightly more proximal lesion with some superficial radial involvement. Incorrect options: (A) Axillary radial nerve injury causes triceps weakness + complete wrist drop + full sensory loss. (C) Spiral groove lesion: triceps spared, wrist drop present (ECRL affected), full posterior forearm sensory loss. (D) Superficial radial nerve at the wrist: purely sensory — dorsal hand and first web space sensory loss only. No motor deficit. Exam pearl: PIN = pure motor. Superficial radial = pure sensory. Radial nerve bifurcates at the elbow into these two.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A pregnant woman presents at 18 weeks for routine anomaly scan. Ultrasonography reveals a sac-like structure over the lumbar spine containing meninges and spinal cord. AFP levels in amniotic fluid are markedly elevated. Which embryological event has failed in this fetus?

options.B: Closure of the posterior neuropore
options.C: Formation of the neural crest cells
options.D: Canalization of the secondary neural tube

questions.explanation: Correct (B): The finding describes myelomeningocele (meninges + spinal cord in the sac). Neural tube closure proceeds from the midpoint cranially (anterior neuropore closes at day 25 → anencephaly if failed) and caudally (posterior neuropore closes at day 27 → lumbar spinal defect if failed). Failure of posterior neuropore closure leads to lumbar/sacral neural tube defects. Elevated AFP in amniotic fluid and maternal serum is a marker of open neural tube defects. Incorrect options: (A) Failure of anterior neuropore closure causes anencephaly, not myelomeningocele. (C) Neural crest cell failure causes defects of the face, peripheral nervous system, adrenal medulla — not open spina bifida. (D) Secondary neural tube formation (canalization) forms the sacral/coccygeal cord; its failure causes a skin-covered defect (spina bifida occulta) or sacral agenesis — not the described lesion. Exam pearl: AFP elevated in open neural tube defects and anterior abdominal wall defects (gastroschisis > omphalocele). Folic acid supplementation reduces neural tube defect risk by 70%.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A muscle biopsy from a patient with Duchenne muscular dystrophy shows absence of a protein that normally connects the intracellular cytoskeleton (actin) to the extracellular matrix. This protein is located in which part of the muscle fiber?

options.B: Sarcolemma (plasma membrane) inner surface
options.D: Z-disc of the sarcomere

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Dystrophin is a large cytoskeletal protein located on the inner surface of the sarcolemma (plasma membrane). It connects intracellular F-actin (via dystrophin-associated protein complex — DAPC) to the extracellular matrix (laminin via dystroglycans). Without dystrophin, mechanical stress during muscle contraction causes membrane tears, calcium influx, and necrosis. Duchenne MD = complete absence of dystrophin (frameshift mutation in DMD gene, X-linked). Incorrect options: (A) T-tubules transmit action potentials and house voltage-gated channels (dihydropyridine receptors) — dystrophin does not primarily reside here. (C) Sarcoplasmic reticulum contains the ryanodine receptor (calcium release channel) and SERCA pump — not dystrophin. (D) Z-discs anchor actin filaments and titin — relevant proteins here include alpha-actinin and desmin, not dystrophin. Exam pearl: Duchenne = no dystrophin (reading frame destroyed). Becker = reduced/altered dystrophin (reading frame preserved). Both X-linked recessive.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 40-year-old woman undergoes a varicose vein stripping procedure. The surgeon ligates the great saphenous vein at the saphenofemoral junction. Which of the following tributaries draining into the great saphenous vein at or near the saphenofemoral junction must the surgeon be aware of?

options.B: Superficial epigastric, superficial circumflex iliac, superficial external pudendal veins
options.C: Lateral circumflex femoral vein, medial circumflex femoral vein
options.D: Profunda femoris vein, deep femoral vein

questions.explanation: Correct (B): At the saphenofemoral junction (SFJ) in the femoral triangle, the great saphenous vein (GSV) receives three important superficial tributaries just before it joins the femoral vein: (1) Superficial epigastric vein, (2) Superficial circumflex iliac vein, (3) Superficial external pudendal vein. These must be individually ligated during saphenofemoral junction ligation to prevent recurrence of varicose veins. Incorrect options: (A) The small saphenous vein drains into the popliteal vein at the popliteal fossa — not at the SFJ. (C) The medial and lateral circumflex femoral veins drain into the profunda femoris (deep femoral vein) — not the GSV at SFJ. (D) Profunda femoris is a DEEP vein — not a tributary of the superficial GSV. Exam pearl: GSV runs from the medial malleolus → medial leg → medial knee → medial thigh → SFJ (4 cm below and lateral to pubic tubercle). It lies anterior to medial malleolus — key landmark for emergency cutdown.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A patient suffers a stroke affecting the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) of the thalamus on the left side. Which visual field defect would be expected?

options.B: Right homonymous hemianopia
options.D: Left monocular visual loss

questions.explanation: Correct (B): The left LGN receives input from: (1) the nasal retina of the right eye (temporal visual field of right eye) via crossed fibers in the optic chiasm, and (2) the temporal retina of the left eye (temporal visual field of left eye — uncrossed fibers). Together, the left LGN processes visual information from the RIGHT visual field of both eyes. Damage to the left LGN → right homonymous hemianopia (loss of right half of visual field in both eyes). Incorrect options: (A) Left homonymous hemianopia would result from right LGN or right optic tract/cortex lesion. (C) Bitemporal hemianopia results from chiasmal lesion (e.g., pituitary adenoma compressing decussating nasal fibers). (D) Monocular visual loss results from pre-chiasmal lesion (optic nerve or retina) of one eye only. Exam pearl: Homonymous defects (same side in both eyes) = post-chiasmal lesion. Optic tract → LGN → optic radiation → visual cortex: all cause contralateral homonymous hemianopia when lesioned. LGN is in the posterior thalamus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 35-year-old primigravida is in prolonged labor. The obstetrician performs a pudendal nerve block by injecting local anesthetic near the ischial spine. Which ligament is the needle directed toward to block the pudendal nerve at this site?

options.B: Sacrotuberous ligament
options.D: Iliolumbar ligament

questions.explanation: Correct (A): The pudendal nerve (S2, S3, S4) exits the greater sciatic foramen below the piriformis, winds around the ischial spine (hooking around the sacrospinous ligament), and re-enters the perineum through the lesser sciatic foramen. The pudendal nerve block is performed by infiltrating local anesthetic just medial to the ischial spine at the attachment of the sacrospinous ligament — the nerve lies just deep and medial to this landmark. This blocks pain from the perineum, vulva, and lower vagina without affecting uterine contractions (uterine innervation is T10–L1, not via pudendal nerve). Incorrect options: (B) Sacrotuberous ligament runs from the sacrum to the ischial tuberosity and forms part of the lesser sciatic notch boundary. The pudendal nerve does pass through this area too, but the classic landmark for block is the sacrospinous ligament and ischial spine. (C) Inguinal ligament is unrelated to the pudendal nerve. (D) Iliolumbar ligament connects the L4–L5 transverse processes to the iliac crest — no relation to pudendal nerve. Exam pearl: Pudendal nerve = S2,3,4 keeps the perineum off the floor. Leaves via greater sciatic foramen, around ischial spine/sacrospinous ligament, enters via lesser sciatic foramen → Alcock's canal.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A newborn is found to have a cystic swelling on the right side of the neck, anterior to the sternocleidomastoid muscle at the junction of its upper and middle thirds. It is soft, fluctuant, and transilluminates. A fistula opens just anterior to the lower sternocleidomastoid. Which pharyngeal pouch is the developmental origin of this lesion?

options.B: 2nd pharyngeal pouch
options.D: 4th pharyngeal pouch

questions.explanation: Correct (B): The description is of a branchial (pharyngeal) cyst and/or fistula. Second branchial cleft cysts are the most common type (95%), located anterior to the sternocleidomastoid at its upper/middle junction. The associated fistula opens externally anterior to the lower third of SCM and internally into the tonsillar fossa. The cyst passes between the internal and external carotid arteries (key surgical landmark). Incorrect options: (A) 1st pharyngeal pouch cysts occur in the preauricular area or parotid region, following the external auditory canal pathway. (C) 3rd pouch cysts occur lower in the neck along the anterior border of lower SCM and are associated with the piriform fossa (internal opening). They are rarer. (D) 4th pouch anomalies are very rare and typically present as thyroid or sinus pyriform fistulae on the left side. Exam pearl: Branchial cyst: cyst between external and internal carotid arteries = 2nd arch. Tonsillar fossa internal opening. Thyroglossal duct cyst: midline, moves with swallowing and tongue protrusion.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: During a hernia repair, the surgeon identifies the inguinal canal. Which of the following correctly describes the boundaries of the deep inguinal ring?

options.A: An opening in the external oblique aponeurosis above the pubic tubercle
options.B: An oval opening in the transversalis fascia, located lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels
options.C: An opening in the internal oblique muscle at the midinguinal point
options.D: A gap between the inguinal ligament and the pectineal ligament

questions.explanation: Correct (B): The deep inguinal ring is an oval defect in the transversalis fascia. It is located approximately at the midpoint of the inguinal ligament (midinguinal point), which is the midpoint between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis — NOT to be confused with the mid-inguinal point which is the midpoint of the inguinal ligament itself. The deep ring is LATERAL to the inferior epigastric vessels (these vessels form the medial boundary/landmark). This is an important surgical and radiological landmark: indirect hernias emerge lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels through the deep ring; direct hernias emerge medial to these vessels through the posterior wall of the inguinal canal (Hesselbach's triangle). Incorrect options: (A) Describes the superficial inguinal ring (opening in external oblique aponeurosis). (C) The internal oblique forms part of the roof of the inguinal canal; it has no ring defect. (D) This gap (lacuna vasorum and musculorum) is related to the femoral canal — not the inguinal ring. Exam pearl: Deep ring = transversalis fascia. Superficial ring = external oblique aponeurosis. Indirect hernia: lateral to epigastrics, through deep ring. Direct: medial to epigastrics, through Hesselbach's triangle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.image_title: Histological section of liver showing hepatic lobule with central vein and portal triad
key_findings: Central vein (terminal hepatic venule) at center
Portal triad at periphery containing portal vein, hepatic artery, bile duct
questions.question_text: A 45-year-old chronic alcoholic develops hepatic necrosis. The histological section of the liver is shown. In right heart failure causing chronic venous congestion (cardiac cirrhosis), which zone of the hepatic acinus (of Rappaport) shows MAXIMAL damage?

options.B: Zone 2 (mid-zonal) — most susceptible to yellow fever
options.C: Zone 3 (centrilobular/perivenular) — most susceptible to ischemia and congestion
options.D: Zone 1 — most susceptible to toxins requiring biotransformation

questions.explanation: Correct (C): Zone 3 (centrilobular zone) is closest to the terminal hepatic venule (central vein) and is the LAST zone to receive oxygenated blood from the portal tracts. In right heart failure (hepatic venous congestion) and in ischemia/hypoxia, Zone 3 suffers the most because: (1) Sinusoidal blood backs up from the central vein outward. (2) It already has the lowest oxygen tension. Nutmeg liver (chronic passive congestion) shows zone 3 necrosis and fibrosis. Incorrect options: (A) Zone 1 (periportal) is MOST oxygenated and MOST susceptible to toxins that are activated by metabolism (e.g., phosphorus poisoning, eclampsia) — NOT to congestion. (B) Zone 2 (midzonal) damage is seen in yellow fever — a classic exam fact. (D) Zone 1 IS susceptible to toxins requiring biotransformation, but this is about congestion, not toxins. Exam pearl: Zone 1 = toxins (phosphorus, eclampsia). Zone 2 = yellow fever. Zone 3 = ischemia, congestion, CCl4 (carbon tetrachloride — requires P450 activation in zone 3), alcohol.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 35-year-old patient develops parotitis (inflammation of the parotid gland). He complains of pain that radiates to the ear. Which nerve transmits this referred pain?

options.B: Auriculotemporal nerve
options.D: Lesser occipital nerve

questions.explanation: Correct (B): The auriculotemporal nerve (branch of the mandibular division of trigeminal, V3) carries sensory innervation from the parotid gland and the skin over the temporal region and the anterior part of the ear (tragus, helix). Inflammation of the parotid refers pain to the ear through this nerve. The auriculotemporal nerve also carries postganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the otic ganglion to the parotid gland (secretomotor). Incorrect options: (A) The facial nerve (CN VII) exits through the stylomastoid foramen and traverses the parotid gland to supply facial muscles — it is a MOTOR nerve to the face and does not carry parotid sensation. (C) Greater auricular nerve (C2, C3) supplies the skin over the angle of mandible and mastoid — it also innervates the lower part of the parotid capsule, but is not the primary referred pain pathway to the ear. (D) Lesser occipital nerve (C2) supplies the scalp behind the ear — not parotid territory. Exam pearl: Auriculotemporal nerve = sensory from parotid + anterior ear + parasympathetic secretomotor to parotid. Frey's syndrome (auriculoparotid fistula): sweating over the cheek during eating due to aberrant regeneration of auriculotemporal nerve into sweat gland territory after parotid surgery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 50-year-old man presents with inability to form new memories (anterograde amnesia) following a surgical complication. Imaging reveals bilateral damage to a specific structure within the medial temporal lobe. Which structure is most likely damaged?

options.B: Hippocampus
options.D: Mammillary bodies

questions.explanation: Correct (B): The hippocampus (within the medial temporal lobe) is critical for the formation of new declarative memories (episodic and semantic). Bilateral hippocampal lesions cause profound anterograde amnesia — the inability to form new long-term memories — as famously demonstrated by patient H.M. (Henry Molaison) following bilateral medial temporal lobectomy. Remote memories (before the lesion) and procedural memory may be preserved. Incorrect options: (A) Amygdala damage: impairs emotional processing (fear conditioning, recognition of emotional facial expressions) — NOT primarily anterograde amnesia. (C) Cingulate gyrus damage: impairs attention, motivation, emotional processing, and executive function — not the classic anterograde amnesia presentation. (D) Mammillary body damage (in Korsakoff's syndrome): causes anterograde AND retrograde amnesia + confabulation — but is due to thiamine deficiency, not the most direct structure for new memory formation. Exam pearl: Hippocampus → declarative (explicit) memory. Amygdala → emotional memory/fear. Cerebellum → procedural memory. Basal ganglia → procedural/implicit learning.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 58-year-old man with superior vena cava (SVC) syndrome develops distended neck veins, facial plethora, and edema of the arms. Which of the following anatomical collateral pathways would be most important for venous drainage from the upper limb to bypass the SVC obstruction?

options.A: Portal venous system via the azygos vein
options.B: Azygos vein → hemiazygos → intercostal veins → inferior vena cava
options.C: Internal mammary vein → inferior epigastric vein → external iliac vein → IVC
options.D: Superior intercostal vein → arch of aorta → descending aorta

questions.explanation: Correct (C): In SVC obstruction, the critical anterior collateral pathway is: Subclavian/axillary vein → internal mammary (internal thoracic) vein → superior epigastric vein → inferior epigastric vein → external iliac vein → common iliac → IVC. This allows blood from the upper limb and head to drain to the IVC bypassing the SVC. Clinically visible as dilated superficial epigastric veins flowing DOWNWARD (toward the groin — opposite of IVC obstruction where flow is upward). Incorrect options: (A) The portal system is not directly connected to the SVC; azygos drains INTO the SVC (so it would be blocked too if SVC is occluded centrally). (B) The azygos/hemiazygos system drains intercostal spaces and ultimately goes to SVC — these would be compromised in high SVC obstruction. (D) Veins cannot drain into the arterial aorta. Exam pearl: SVC syndrome collaterals: epigastric veins flow DOWNWARD. IVC obstruction: epigastric veins flow UPWARD. Caval obstruction: epigastric veins flow toward patent side.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 55-year-old man with carcinoma of the head of pancreas presents with progressive jaundice, pale stools, and dark urine. The tumor is compressing a specific bile duct structure. Which anatomical relationship explains why cancer of the pancreatic head causes obstructive jaundice?

options.A: The common hepatic duct runs within the head of pancreas
options.B: The common bile duct runs in a groove on the posterior surface of the head of pancreas
options.C: The cystic duct crosses posterior to the head of pancreas
options.D: The right hepatic duct passes through the neck of pancreas

questions.explanation: Correct (B): The common bile duct (CBD) descends in a groove or tunnel in the posterior aspect of the head of the pancreas before joining the pancreatic duct of Wirsung and opening into the second part of the duodenum at the ampulla of Vater (hepatopancreatic ampulla). A malignant tumor in the pancreatic head compresses or invades the CBD → bile cannot drain → obstructive jaundice (painless, progressive, with pale stools and dark urine). This presentation (Courvoisier's sign: palpable, non-tender gallbladder + jaundice) is a surgical emergency. Incorrect options: (A) The common HEPATIC duct is formed by union of right and left hepatic ducts in the porta hepatis — it does NOT enter the pancreas. It joins the cystic duct to form the CBD. (C) The cystic duct connects the gallbladder to the common hepatic duct in the hepatoduodenal ligament — it does not cross the pancreas. (D) The right hepatic duct is entirely within the liver hilum. Exam pearl: Courvoisier's law: Painless progressive jaundice + palpable gallbladder = malignant CBD obstruction (NOT gallstones, as chronic stone disease causes gallbladder fibrosis and it cannot distend).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A full-term neonate develops cyanosis immediately after birth. Echocardiogram shows the aorta arising from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery arising from the left ventricle. Oxygenated and deoxygenated blood circulate in parallel. Which embryological abnormality is responsible?

options.A: Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral (non-spiral aorticopulmonary septum)
options.B: Abnormal position of the bulbus cordis
options.C: Failure of closure of the foramen ovale
options.D: Incomplete development of the endocardial cushions

questions.explanation: Correct (A): Transposition of the Great Arteries (TGA) results from failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral as it partitions the truncus arteriosus. Normally, the septum spirals ~180° so that the aorta ends up above the left ventricle and the pulmonary trunk above the right ventricle. If the septum does NOT spiral (grows straight), the aorta arises from the RV (receives deoxygenated blood) and the pulmonary trunk from the LV (receives oxygenated blood) — creating parallel (not series) circulations. This is incompatible with life unless mixing occurs (PDA, ASD, VSD). Incorrect options: (B) Abnormal bulbus cordis position contributes to dextrocardia or other situs anomalies — not TGA. (C) Failure of foramen ovale closure = ASD (patent foramen ovale) — causes left-to-right shunt; not TGA. (D) Endocardial cushion defects → AV canal defects (ASD + VSD + AV valve abnormalities). Exam pearl: TGA = non-spiral aorticopulmonary septum. Truncus arteriosus = no aorticopulmonary septum. Both involve the spiral septum at different levels of failure.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 28-year-old man develops DI (diabetes insipidus) with polyuria and dilute urine after a head injury involving the base of the skull. Lesion in which hypothalamic nucleus is most likely responsible?

options.B: Lateral hypothalamic nucleus
options.D: Preoptic nucleus

questions.explanation: Correct (C): ADH (vasopressin) is synthesized in the supraoptic nuclei and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus. It is transported down axons of the hypothalamohypophyseal tract to be stored and released from the posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis). Damage to these nuclei or their axons (e.g., head injury, craniopharyngioma, surgery) reduces ADH production → diabetes insipidus (large volumes of dilute urine, polydipsia). Incorrect options: (A) Ventromedial nucleus is the satiety center — its damage causes hyperphagia and obesity. (B) Lateral hypothalamic nucleus is the hunger/feeding center — its damage causes anorexia and weight loss. (D) Preoptic nucleus contains the sexually dimorphic nucleus (involved in reproductive behavior) and thermoregulation centers — not ADH production. Exam pearl: Hypothalamic nuclei memory: Supraoptic = ADH. Paraventricular = ADH + oxytocin. Preoptic = temperature. Ventromedial = satiety (destroy = fat). Lateral = hunger (destroy = thin). Suprachiasmatic = circadian rhythm.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 45-year-old diabetic man presents with a foot drop that developed insidiously over months. Nerve conduction studies show reduced conduction at the fibular head. He does not recall any trauma. What is the most likely cause and involved nerve?

options.A: Tarsal tunnel syndrome compressing the tibial nerve
options.B: Common peroneal nerve compression at the fibular neck due to habitual leg crossing
options.C: Sciatic nerve entrapment at the piriformis (piriformis syndrome)
options.D: Femoral nerve compression at the inguinal ligament

questions.explanation: Correct (B): The common peroneal (fibular) nerve wraps around the neck/head of the fibula where it is extremely superficial and susceptible to compression. Causes include: habitual leg crossing, prolonged squatting, tight casts, and diabetes (mononeuritis multiplex). It presents with foot drop (weakness of dorsiflexion and eversion), sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot and anterolateral leg, and NCS showing slowing at the fibular head. Incorrect options: (A) Tarsal tunnel syndrome compresses the tibial nerve behind the medial malleolus → plantar foot pain and numbness + toe flexion weakness — not foot drop. (C) Piriformis syndrome compresses the sciatic nerve → buttock pain with radiation down the leg, worse on internal rotation of hip — not isolated foot drop with fibular head NCS abnormality. (D) Femoral nerve compression → quadriceps weakness and anterior thigh sensory loss — not foot drop. Exam pearl: Common peroneal nerve = most superficial and most commonly compressed nerve in the lower limb. NCS localizes the lesion to the fibular head. Treatment: avoid compression, physiotherapy, occasionally surgical decompression.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 10-year-old boy presents with hematuria and proteinuria. Kidney biopsy on electron microscopy shows effacement (fusion) of the foot processes of glomerular visceral epithelial cells. Which cell type is affected?

options.B: Podocytes (visceral epithelial cells)
options.D: Parietal epithelial cells of Bowman's capsule

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Podocytes (visceral epithelial cells) form the outer layer of the glomerular filtration barrier. Their foot processes (pedicels) interdigitate and are connected by slit diaphragms — the critical size-selective filtration barrier for proteins. Effacement (fusion) of foot processes on EM is the hallmark of minimal change disease (MCD), the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children. Podocyte injury → loss of the slit diaphragm → heavy proteinuria → nephrotic syndrome. Incorrect options: (A) Mesangial cells provide structural support, regulate glomerular filtration, and are involved in IgA nephropathy (IgA deposits in mesangium). (C) Juxtaglomerular cells (granular cells) are modified smooth muscle cells in the afferent arteriole that produce renin. (D) Parietal epithelial cells line Bowman's capsule; they are involved in crescent formation in rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis — not foot process effacement. Exam pearl: MCD: foot process effacement on EM, no deposits on LM/IF, responds to steroids, most common childhood nephrotic syndrome.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 42-year-old man with portal hypertension develops massive hematemesis. Endoscopy reveals esophageal varices in the lower third of the esophagus. These varices are formed by dilation of which anastomotic venous pathway?

options.A: Left gastric vein (portal) anastomosing with esophageal veins (systemic, draining to azygos/hemiazygos)
options.B: Right gastric vein (portal) anastomosing with intercostal veins
options.C: Inferior mesenteric vein (portal) with inferior rectal vein (systemic)
options.D: Paraumbilical veins (portal) with superior epigastric vein (systemic)

questions.explanation: Correct (A): The left gastric vein (coronary vein) of the portal system anastomoses with the esophageal tributaries of the azygos and hemiazygos veins (systemic). In portal hypertension, this portosystemic anastomosis dilates forming esophageal varices — the most dangerous complication (bleeding risk ~30%). Incorrect options: (B) Right gastric vein does not form significant esophageal varices — it drains to the portal vein directly. (C) Inferior mesenteric vein anastomosing with inferior rectal vein (systemic) forms anorectal varices (hemorrhoids) — not esophageal varices. (D) Paraumbilical veins anastomosing with epigastric veins (systemic) form the caput medusae — dilated superficial abdominal veins around the umbilicus — not esophageal varices. Exam pearl: Portosystemic anastomoses: (1) Esophageal varices = left gastric + esophageal veins. (2) Anorectal varices = superior rectal (IMV/portal) + middle/inferior rectal (internal iliac/systemic). (3) Caput medusae = paraumbilical + epigastric. (4) Retroperitoneal = Retzius veins.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 55-year-old man presents with ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis of the right side of the face. There is no anhydrosis of the upper limb. Where is the most likely site of the lesion in the sympathetic pathway?

options.A: Central (first-order) — hypothalamus to T1 lateral horn
options.B: Preganglionic (second-order) — T1 to superior cervical ganglion, involving the apex of lung
options.C: Postganglionic (third-order) — along the internal carotid artery to the eye
options.D: Postganglionic — along the external carotid artery, causing isolated anhidrosis of the face

questions.explanation: Correct (C): Horner's syndrome = ptosis + miosis + anhidrosis (enophthalmos). The DISTRIBUTION of anhidrosis localizes the lesion: (1) Central (hypothalamus to T1): Anhidrosis of entire ipsilateral body. (2) Preganglionic (T1 to superior cervical ganglion — e.g., Pancoast tumor at lung apex): Anhidrosis of face AND arm (because sudomotor fibers to face and arm both travel with preganglionic fibers). (3) Postganglionic along INTERNAL carotid: Anhidrosis of FACE ONLY (without upper limb) — because the arm's sudomotor fibers diverge at the SCG and travel with the subclavian artery. FACE ONLY with NO arm involvement = internal carotid artery territory (third-order neuron). (4) Postganglionic along EXTERNAL carotid: Isolated facial anhidrosis without ptosis/miosis — different presentation. Incorrect options: (A) Central lesion causes whole body (ipsilateral) anhidrosis. (B) Pancoast (preganglionic at lung apex): face AND arm anhidrosis. (D) External carotid lesion causes isolated anhidrosis without ptosis or miosis — not the described scenario. Exam pearl: Localize Horner's by anhidrosis pattern. ICA = only face anhidrosis + ptosis + miosis. Pancoast = face + arm + ptosis + miosis + also pain from brachial plexus involvement.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 30-year-old trauma patient requires emergency pericardiocentesis. The needle is inserted subxiphoidally and directed toward the left shoulder. Through which structures does the needle pass BEFORE entering the pericardial sac?

options.A: Skin → subcutaneous tissue → sternum → fibrous pericardium
options.B: Skin → subcutaneous tissue → rectus abdominis → diaphragm → fibrous pericardium
options.C: Skin → subcutaneous tissue → linea alba → transversalis fascia → fibrous pericardium
options.D: Skin → subcutaneous tissue → right intercostal space → parietal pleura → fibrous pericardium

questions.explanation: Correct (B): The subxiphoid (subxiphysternal) approach to pericardiocentesis: needle enters below the xiphoid process at 45° angle toward the left shoulder. It passes through: skin → subcutaneous fat → linea alba/rectus sheath → the anterior surface of the diaphragm (the central tendon or muscular part) → then into the pericardial sac (fibrous then serous pericardium). The diaphragm is a key layer traversed in this approach. Incorrect options: (A) Through the sternum would require a sternal saw — this is a surgical sternotomy approach, not needle pericardiocentesis. (C) Transversalis fascia is the endoabdominal fascia — it is crossed, but the diaphragm is the critical structure not mentioned. (D) The right intercostal approach is an alternative route but is at risk of injuring the pleura and lung; the subxiphoid approach specifically avoids the pleura. Exam pearl: Subxiphoid pericardiocentesis: preferred because it avoids pleural cavities. Directed at left shoulder to avoid liver (right) and heart musculature. ECG guidance (ST elevation when needle touches myocardium) used to confirm position.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A woman takes thalidomide in the 4th to 7th week of pregnancy without knowing she is pregnant. The baby is born with complete absence of the limbs (amelia). Which embryological structure is responsible for inducing limb bud outgrowth?

options.B: Apical ectodermal ridge (AER)
options.D: Neural crest cells

questions.explanation: Correct (B): The Apical Ectodermal Ridge (AER) is a thickened ridge of ectoderm at the tip of the limb bud. It produces FGF-4 and FGF-8 (fibroblast growth factors), which are essential for PROXIMAL-TO-DISTAL outgrowth (elongation) of the limb. Thalidomide (an anti-angiogenic/teratogenic drug) disrupts AER-mesenchymal signaling, causing amelia (complete limb absence) or phocomelia (seal limbs) depending on timing. Incorrect options: (A) ZPA (Zone of Polarizing Activity) is located at the posterior margin of the limb bud. It produces Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) and controls ANTERO-POSTERIOR (radial-ulnar/tibular-fibular) patterning. ZPA damage → digit patterning defects, not amelia. (C) Notochord is the central axis of the embryo providing the primary organizing signal for dorsal induction — not limb bud outgrowth. (D) Neural crest cells contribute to the face, peripheral nervous system, melanocytes, and heart septa — not limb bud outgrowth. Exam pearl: AER → proximo-distal axis (FGF). ZPA → antero-posterior axis (SHH). Dorsal ectoderm → dorso-ventral axis (Wnt7a). AER removal at different time points: early = amelia; mid = loss of distal elements.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.image_title: Peripheral blood smear showing abnormal red cell morphology
key_findings: Nucleated red blood cells in some fields
questions.question_text: A 16-year-old African boy presents with severe bone pain crises and the peripheral blood smear shown above. The pathological RBCs in this condition result from which molecular defect?

options.A: Deletion of alpha-globin genes causing excess beta chains
options.B: Point mutation in beta-globin gene: glutamic acid → valine at position 6
options.C: Point mutation in alpha-globin gene: glutamic acid → lysine at position 6
options.D: Deficiency of spectrin leading to membrane fragility

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Sickle cell disease (HbS) results from a single point mutation in the beta-globin gene (GAG → GTG), replacing glutamic acid (hydrophilic) with valine (hydrophobic) at position 6. This creates a hydrophobic patch on the deoxygenated HbS molecule, causing polymerization and sickling. The smear shows classic sickle-shaped RBCs, target cells, and evidence of hyposplenism in a chronic disease patient. Incorrect options: (A) Alpha-globin gene deletions cause alpha-thalassemia (excess beta chains form HbH = β4 tetramers or in newborns, Hb Barts = γ4) — not sickle cell disease. (C) Glutamic acid → lysine substitution at position 6 of the alpha chain describes HbC disease (actually HbC is in the beta chain — glutamic acid → lysine at beta-6). This is a different hemoglobinopathy (HbC) distinct from HbS. (D) Spectrin deficiency causes hereditary spherocytosis — spherocytes, osmotic fragility, not sickle cells. Exam pearl: HbS = Glu→Val at beta-6 (hydrophilic→hydrophobic). Sickling precipitated by: hypoxia, acidosis, dehydration, cold, infection.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A urologist performs a transurethral prostatectomy. He notes that the prostate gland has a true capsule and a false capsule. The surgical approach involves the zone most commonly affected by benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). Which zone is this?

options.B: Central zone
options.D: Anterior fibromuscular stroma

questions.explanation: Correct (C): The prostate has four zones (McNeal's classification): (1) Peripheral zone (70% of glandular tissue) — most common site of prostate CANCER. (2) Central zone (25%) — surrounds ejaculatory ducts; site of central zone carcinoma (uncommon). (3) Transitional zone (5%) — surrounds the proximal urethra; site of BENIGN PROSTATIC HYPERPLASIA (BPH). The enlarged transitional zone compresses the urethra, causing lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS). (4) Anterior fibromuscular stroma — non-glandular. Incorrect options: (A) Peripheral zone is the most common site of prostate CANCER — NOT BPH. DRE palpates the peripheral zone. (B) Central zone is less commonly affected by either BPH or cancer. (D) Anterior fibromuscular stroma is non-glandular and not involved in either BPH or cancer. Exam pearl: BPH = Transitional zone. Cancer = Peripheral zone. DRE detects PERIPHERAL zone nodules. PSA elevated in both BPH and cancer.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A right-handed 65-year-old man develops fluent speech with normal prosody and flow but cannot understand spoken or written language. He also cannot repeat phrases. He is unaware of his comprehension deficit (anosognosia). Where is the most likely lesion?

options.A: Left Broca's area (inferior frontal gyrus, BA 44, 45)
options.B: Left Wernicke's area (posterior superior temporal gyrus, BA 22)
options.D: Right hemisphere diffuse lesion

questions.explanation: Correct (B): The presentation describes Wernicke's aphasia: fluent speech (production intact), severely impaired comprehension, impaired repetition, paraphasias (wrong words), and lack of awareness of deficit (anosognosia). Wernicke's area (left posterior superior temporal gyrus, Brodmann area 22) is the receptive language area. Its damage impairs comprehension of language (spoken and written). Incorrect options: (A) Broca's area damage (left inferior frontal gyrus) causes Broca's aphasia: non-fluent, effortful speech with preserved comprehension. Patient is aware and frustrated. (C) Arcuate fasciculus lesion connecting Broca's and Wernicke's areas causes conduction aphasia: fluent speech, good comprehension, but IMPAIRED REPETITION with intact comprehension — different from Wernicke's where comprehension is also affected. (D) Right hemisphere lesions in a right-hander cause impaired prosody (aprosodia) — the emotional and musical quality of speech — but not classic aphasia. Exam pearl: Broca's = non-fluent, good comprehension. Wernicke's = fluent, poor comprehension. Conduction = fluent, good comprehension, poor repetition. Global = all functions impaired.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 40-year-old man develops ipsilateral facial pain (V1, V2, V3 distribution), diplopia (CN VI palsy), proptosis, and chemosis of the right eye. He is febrile and unwell. CT shows thrombus in a venous structure adjacent to the sphenoid bone. Which venous structure is most likely involved?

options.B: Cavernous sinus
options.D: Inferior petrosal sinus

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Cavernous sinus thrombosis (CST) presents with: (1) Proptosis, chemosis, periorbital edema (venous congestion), (2) Painful ophthalmoplegia (CN III, IV, VI palsy — especially CN VI palsy most commonly), (3) Facial pain/numbness (V1, V2 — via ophthalmic and maxillary divisions of trigeminal nerve which run in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus), (4) Fever and toxicity (usually from septic thrombosis, e.g., Staph aureus from facial boil in the 'danger zone'). The cavernous sinus lies on either side of the sella turcica adjacent to the sphenoid bone. Incorrect options: (A) Superior sagittal sinus thrombosis: headache, papilledema, seizures, focal neurological deficits — NOT proptosis/ophthalmoplegia. (C) Sigmoid sinus thrombosis: complicates mastoiditis; presents with Gradenigo syndrome (ipsilateral CN VI palsy + facial pain in V1 from petrous apex involvement). (D) Inferior petrosal sinus: drains the cavernous sinus; its thrombosis is secondary to CS thrombosis. Exam pearl: Cavernous sinus contents — 'TOM CAT': Trochlear, Oculomotor, Maxillary (V2), CN VI (inside, most medial), Abducens, Trigeminal V1 (ophthalmic). CN VI most commonly affected first as it is least protected (inside sinus, not in wall).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 50-year-old man with carcinoma of the descending colon undergoes left hemicolectomy. Which artery is ligated during this procedure, and from which main vessel does it originate?

options.A: Right colic artery from superior mesenteric artery
options.B: Left colic artery from inferior mesenteric artery
options.C: Middle colic artery from superior mesenteric artery
options.D: Sigmoid arteries from superior mesenteric artery

questions.explanation: Correct (B): The descending colon (from the left colic flexure to the sigmoid colon) is supplied by the left colic artery, which arises from the inferior mesenteric artery (IMA). During left hemicolectomy, the IMA or the left colic artery is ligated. The marginal artery of Drummond may provide collateral flow. Incorrect options: (A) Right colic artery (from SMA) supplies the ascending colon — relevant to right hemicolectomy. (C) Middle colic artery (from SMA) supplies the transverse colon — ligated during transverse colectomy or extended right hemicolectomy. (D) Sigmoid arteries arise from the IMA (not SMA) and supply the sigmoid colon — relevant to sigmoid colectomy, not exclusively left hemicolectomy. Exam pearl: Midgut (SMA territory): From distal duodenum → cecum → ascending colon → proximal two-thirds of transverse colon. Hindgut (IMA territory): Distal transverse → descending → sigmoid → upper rectum. Watershed areas: Splenic flexure (SMA/IMA junction) and rectosigmoid junction — most vulnerable to ischemia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 25-year-old woman with secondary amenorrhea is found to have markedly elevated FSH and LH. Ovarian biopsy shows absence of follicles with fibrotic streaks. Which cells of the ovary produce estrogen in a normal reproductive-age woman?

options.A: Theca interna cells produce estrogen directly
options.B: Granulosa cells aromatize androgens (from theca interna) to estrogen
options.C: Corpus luteum granulosa-lutein cells produce estrogen only
options.D: Stromal interstitial cells produce estrogen independently

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Estrogen production is a TWO-CELL, TWO-GONADOTROPIN process: (1) LH stimulates THECA INTERNA cells to produce androgens (androstenedione, testosterone) via the cholesterol → pregnenolone pathway. (2) FSH stimulates GRANULOSA CELLS to express aromatase (CYP19A1), which converts these androgens into estrogens (estradiol, estrone). Granulosa cells cannot synthesize androgens de novo (lack 17-hydroxylase), and theca cells cannot aromatize androgens (lack aromatase in normal conditions). This collaborative two-cell model is fundamental to reproductive biology. Incorrect options: (A) Theca interna cells produce ANDROGENS (androstenedione), not estrogen directly. They are stimulated by LH. (C) Corpus luteum produces primarily PROGESTERONE (from granulosa-lutein cells) and some estrogen. (D) Stromal cells produce androgens (DHEA, androstenedione) but not primary estrogen. Exam pearl: Two-cell theory: Theca (LH) → androgens → Granulosa (FSH+aromatase) → estrogens. In PCOS: excess LH → excess androgens → impaired aromatization → hyperandrogenism + anovulation.
